To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(1) the 4 major categories of asteroid activities—scientific research (Science), human settlement of space (Settlement), planetary defense, and mining (Sales)—are best served, respectively, by (2) a policy regime that is open to all actors, (3) a policy regime in which the government has a dominant role, (4) a policy regime with a dominant public-private partnership, and (5) a policy regime focused on private actors.

1) asteroid activities can be classified into 4 categories—science, settlement, security, and sales—and each category is best served by a different set of policy arrangements, 2) the different policy needs of the 4 categories are not compatible and present policymakers with tradeoffs, and 3) the tradeoffs are best understood in the context of 3 different types of policy goals that are pursued by different actors—scientific, security, and settlement.

4 main categories (science, settlement, security, and sales) of activities envisioned for asteroid activities have distinct features, which are not mutually supportive and are best served by different policy regimes.
In summary, our research is concerned with

the policy needs of asteroid activities that are not necessarily compatible with the policy needs for other types of asteroid activities, and we argue for a more nuanced understanding of the policy needs of different asteroid activities.
how policymakers can best balance different goals and needs to achieve an optimal policy outcome.

how the different policy regimes that serve distinct goals are likely to affect the pace of progress in the 4 main asteroid activities and how these policy regimes may affect the development of the broader space sector.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
asteroid activities should be pursued in a manner that maximizes the benefits and minimizes the costs to humanity.
the current asteroid activities are not necessarily compatible, and thus the current policies should not be designed in a way to serve them simultaneously.
the current policy environment is not well designed to enable the full spectrum of activities envisioned for asteroids, and that the current policy regime is not well designed for asteroid science.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
asteroid mining, planetary defense, and human settlement are best pursued by different policy regimes than those that are best for science.
a policy that is good for one type of asteroid activity may not be good for other types.
the policy regime for each activity should be based on the goals of each activity.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the different goals of asteroid actors are in tension, not harmony.

policymakers must be careful to ensure that their asteroid policy is well tailored to the activities they are seeking to enable, rather than simply adopting a policy that is a “one size fits all” solution.
policymakers should consider the trade-offs inherent in asteroid policies, and that they should consider how to manage the trade-offs in a manner that best serves the public interest.
